<reason>A high-quality, genuinely contested debate. B landed the sharpest technical hits: the harmless obligation-free review workflow, the dilemma in A's functional "funnel" definition, and the contradiction between "categorical display means nobody decides" and A's reliance on conspicuousness standards. But A's path to the motion stayed more direct and its harms were never fully neutralized: B's alternative package concededly lacks pre-checkout itemization and full rules display, and its defenses of those gaps (itemization doesn't change affordability; enforceable materiality standards) were pressed hard and only partially held. B's affirmative stake — staging flexibility and attention management — was thinner than A's concrete consumer harms, and B's own package requires at least as much interpretive enforcement as the bright line it criticized. A's closing delivered the cleanest weighing device of the debate: the mandate's failure mode is redundancy, while the alternative's failure mode is unremedied late disclosure litigated definition-by-definition, and the speed-limit analogy honestly absorbed the harmless-click concession. Competitive throughout, but A gave the clearer reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.5–B4.8): exposing that A's functional funnel definition arguably permits B's obligation-free review screen, and that "categorical display means nobody decides" contradicts A's own reliance on conspicuousness judgments. The most damaging single exchange; A never squarely repaired it, surviving only by re-weighing on error costs in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
